historical_timeline.summary: Born Ray Charles Robinson in Albany, Georgia.
Began to lose his sight; his younger brother drowned the same year.
Blind by age seven; enrolled at the Florida School for the Deaf and Blind.
Arrested for heroin possession; later admitted addiction since the late 1940s.
Stopped heroin after rehabilitation at a California sanitarium.
Died at his home in Beverly Hills.

claims.statement: Ray Charles Robinson was born in Albany, Georgia, on September 23, 1930; his mother moved him as an infant to Greenville, a small town in north Florida.
Ray Charles died at his home in Beverly Hills, California, on June 10, 2004, of acute liver disease, according to his spokesman.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail; the episode records no liver diagnosis.

claims.statement: Charles began to lose his sight at about age five and was blind by age seven; after he was declared legally blind, he was enrolled at the Florida School for the Deaf and Blind in St. Augustine, where he remained for nine years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the blindness of both eyes since childhood. The sources do not grade the residual vision; the record treats it as total blindness.

claims.statement: The cause of his blindness is uncertain. It is described as probably congenital juvenile glaucoma, and glaucoma is often mentioned as the cause, but Charles said that nothing was ever diagnosed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; glaucoma is not coded as a diagnosis.

claims.statement: In 1964 Charles was arrested for possession of heroin, and he later admitted that he had been addicted since the late 1940s. After a period of rehabilitation at a California sanitarium he stopped using drugs and received a five-year suspended sentence.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public admission and the documented rehabilitation; the anchor for the synthetic opioid use disorder in sustained remission.

claims.statement: Charles struggled with heroin addiction for nearly 20 years and quit "cold turkey" in 1965, after an arrest at the Boston airport. He later became reluctant to discuss his drug use, fearing it would taint how people viewed his work.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports the long remission and the recovery-oriented, non-stigmatizing approach in the episode.

claims.statement: In the year Charles began to lose his sight, his younger brother drowned. His mother died in 1945.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; no cause of the mother's death is given.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Disability-competent primary care for a man blind since childhood (introductions and spoken orientation, describing each step of the examination, accessible electronic documents, braille and audio medication labels, and fall prevention), recovery-oriented care for an opioid use disorder in sustained remission for three decades (naloxone, relapse-prevention discussion, and a plan for any future pain that protects his recovery, in non-stigmatizing language), depression screening and a structured safety assessment, and eye care for blind eyes limited to what can help him (comfort, pain, and the place of pressure checks) on the CMID glaucoma and depression monographs with AAO, ASAM, and VA/DoD guidance.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Charles is a 65-year-old man, blind since childhood, with an opioid use disorder in sustained remission for more than thirty years, who returns four weeks after his first visit and is seen by ophthalmology on the same day. His eyes have been comfortable, with no pain, redness, discharge, or headache around the eyes. He picked up the naloxone nasal spray; the pharmacy put a braille label on the box and now gives audio labels for any medicine. He received his first-visit summary and results as an accessible electronic document and read them with his screen reader. He has had no opioid or other drug use and no cravings, and he has been touring as usual. He has had no falls.

He keeps one naloxone spray at home and one in his travel bag, and the people he travels with have been shown how to use it. He has had no opioid or other drug use and no cravings, including on long tours and in hotel rooms, which he names as the times he is most careful. His eyes have been comfortable. He has had no falls; in hotels he is shown around each new room on arrival and keeps his belongings in fixed places. He has started working on a plan for any future pain with Dr. Fenwick.

documentation.advance_care_planning: Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with his consent. He named a health care agent, and a health care proxy form was completed; the agent is recorded in the chart and is not named here. The form was read aloud to him in full before he signed it, and he was given an accessible electronic copy. He said that what matters most to him is staying independent, keeping up his work, and protecting his recovery, and that he wants to be asked directly, not through others, about any medicine that could affect it. He chose not to record specific treatment preferences today. The plan will be revisited yearly or after any serious illness.
documentation.follow_up: Chronic-care review in three months, with the first zoster dose and the Tdap booster. Test results sent to him as accessible electronic messages. Yearly ophthalmology review in the spring. Next annual wellness visit in one year

referral.question: Blindness of both eyes since early childhood, with no light perception, in a 65-year-old man new to the practice. The cause was never diagnosed; glaucoma is often suggested. Please examine the eyes for comfort and complications and advise whether eye pressure needs checking or treatment, and what eye care he needs from here
referral.urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as his four-week primary care check
referral.pertinent_history: Gradual loss of sight from about age five, blind by age seven; no eye care on record in recent years. No light perception today. He reports no eye pain, redness, discharge, or headache around the eyes, and uses no eye drops. Lids and ocular surfaces look quiet on primary care examination. Independent in all daily activities using nonvisual methods and a screen reader. Opioid use disorder in sustained remission for more than thirty years without medication; naloxone nasal spray prescribed today. PHQ-9 2. No other medicines. Please send the report as an accessible electronic document; he reads with a screen reader, and he asks that each step of the examination be described before it is done
questions: Is there any active eye disease, such as inflammation, exposure, or raised pressure causing pain, that needs treatment now?
In eyes with no light perception and no pain, should eye pressure be measured or lowered?
What eye surveillance does he need, and how often?
Which symptoms should bring him back urgently?
Would any vision rehabilitation services help him now?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Charles, a 65-year-old man, is seen at the request of Dr. Fenwick. He lost his sight gradually from about age five and was blind by age seven; he says no cause was ever diagnosed. He has no eye pain, redness, discharge, light sensitivity, or headache around the eyes, and he uses no eye drops. He wears dark glasses by habit. He is independent in all daily activities, travels for work with a sighted guide in unfamiliar places, and reads with a screen reader
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Fenwick's first-visit note four weeks ago, including the history, examination, PHQ-9, and medicine list, and today's primary care eye findings

exam.finding: No light perception on either side
Dark glasses removed with his permission. Lids, lashes, and periocular skin normal; no swelling, redness, or discharge; lids close fully
Quiet on both sides, with no injection, exposure, or discharge
None on gentle palpation over either eye
Not measured: in comfortable eyes with no light perception, the reading would not change care

assessment.display: Blindness of both eyes since childhood, no light perception
assessment.assessment: Comfortable, quiet eyes with no active disease. The cause of the childhood blindness cannot be settled from today's examination; congenital or juvenile glaucoma is often suggested, but no diagnosis was ever made and none is recorded now. There is no inflammation, exposure, or sign of painful raised pressure

assessment.display: Eye pressure in blind, painless eyes
assessment.assessment: Lowering eye pressure protects sight that remains; with no light perception there is no sight to protect. In a painless eye, pressure checks and drops would add burden without benefit. Pressure matters again only if the eye becomes painful or red, when it may need treatment for comfort
A yearly comfort-focused eye examination is enough, with earlier review for symptoms. Optic nerve imaging, visual fields, gonioscopy, and corneal thickness would not change his care
He has long-established nonvisual skills and the technology he needs. Services remain open to him if his needs change

recommendations: No eye drops or other eye treatment now
No routine eye pressure checks, optic nerve imaging, or visual fields
Yearly ophthalmology review focused on comfort and the ocular surface
Same-day review for eye pain, redness, discharge, swelling, light sensitivity, or headache around the eye, so that a painful blind eye can be treated promptly
Primary care to ask about eye comfort at each visit
Vision rehabilitation services (orientation and mobility, assistive technology) offered today; he does not want them now and can ask at any time
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Fenwick, who sees him the same day. The findings and plan were explained to Mr. Charles, who agreed with them, and this report was sent to him as an accessible electronic document
consultant_note.follow_up: Ophthalmology review in one year, or the same day for eye pain or redness
